audit_notes: Parameters positive and within bounds. The model represents a polymer-induced log-law shift Delta U+ = 4.3 as an effective slip length b = Delta U+ * delta_nu = 20.6 um in a Couette gap calibrated to H+ = U_b+/2 = 18.3 (H = 88 um); this reproduces the linearised turbulent result DR ~ 2 Delta U+/U_b+ and gives b/(H+b) = 19.0 % wall-shear reduction. The calibration is sound for small shifts; for Delta U+ = 4.3 the linearisation is still within a few percent of the exact Cf ratio (36.5/40.8)^2 = 0.80. Physical plausibility: flat-plate and ship-model polymer injection (PEO, 1000-4000 wppm injectate) has demonstrated local DR of 60-80 % decaying to 10-30 % over ~10 m, so a hull average of ~20 % with injection rows every ~10 m is plausible but not conservative; polymer chain scission at high wall shear (tau_w = 50 Pa) and in the injection pores reduces effectiveness over the first metres. The concept passes the physical audit, but its two practical weaknesses are severe and are recorded here: (1) consumption of order 4 t/day of polymer for a 200 m ship at 8 m/s, which at 3-5 EUR/kg (12-20 kEUR/day) exceeds the fuel saving of a 20 % skin-friction reduction (~14 % fuel, ~3-6 kEUR/day for a 40-60 t/day ship) by a factor of 3-5, and discharges this polymer into the sea (non-toxic but not negligible); (2) it has no antifouling function, so it does not answer the non-toxic antifouling part of the request and would have to be combined with a fouling-release coating. Structural: 10 um pores in the coating are mechanically unproblematic but clog with biofilm unless kept flowing. Baseline: the same smooth hull without polymer release (log_law_shift = 0).
